definition: Demarcation means the marking of a clear boundary or dividing line between two things.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word demarcation. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know demarcation should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The surveyor drove bright orange stakes along the property line, and that demarcation finally ended the neighbors' argument over where one yard stopped and the other began.
A distinction is weaker — it notes a difference between two things without demarcation's sense of an explicitly drawn, marked-out line.
A gulf is stronger than a demarcation — it implies a vast, hard-to-bridge separation between two things, far beyond a line that has simply been drawn and labeled.

Delineation is the precise outlining or describing of something's limits — a job description delineates duties, a sketch delineates a coastline. It is the act of drawing or spelling out. Demarcation is the established dividing line itself, fixed and marked between two things. You produce a delineation on paper; a demarcation stands on the ground.

A boundary is any line that marks the limit of an area or category — a fence, a county line, a personal limit — whether or not anyone marked it deliberately. Demarcation stresses the deliberate act and its result: the line is explicitly drawn and marked, so the two sides are set apart beyond argument.

The borderline is the line where one thing ends and another begins, and the word often shades into 'almost' — a borderline case sits right at the edge of a category. Demarcation is firmer and more formal: a dividing line explicitly drawn and marked out so the two sides cannot be confused.

Demarcation means the marking of a clear boundary or dividing line between two things.
The textbook uses the invention of the printing press as its demarcation between the medieval period and the early modern era.

Demarcation fits because the printing press serves as a clear dividing line between two categories of history — everything before it belongs to one era, everything after it to another, with the boundary explicitly marked.

Demarcation shows up in law, labor, geography, and formal writing — often in the set phrases 'line of demarcation' and 'demarcation dispute' (a labor term for arguments over which workers may do which jobs).
In casual speech, people just say 'dividing line' or 'boundary.'

For three generations, the two fishing villages quarreled over where one's waters ended and the other's began.
Nets were cut, catches disputed, and every season reopened the argument.
Then a fisheries officer anchored a row of white buoys across the bay, each one numbered and charted.
The demarcation changed almost nothing about the fish and almost everything about the peace.
With the line visibly marked, a skipper could no longer claim an honest mistake, and the quarrels quietly ended.
